newsitem.title: USA: US GDP grew nearly 6 pct in Q1--Commerce's Ehrlich.
newsitem.headline: US GDP grew nearly 6 pct in Q1--Commerce's Ehrlich.

text.p: The U.S. economy looks to have grown at very close to a six percent annualized pace in the first quarter, Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich said on Wednesday.
"It smells like six percent," Ehrlich told a news conference after publication of the March trade data.
The Commerce Department originally reported that gross domestic product expanded by 5.6 percent in the first quarter, its fastest pace in more than nine years.
But Ehrlich said subsequent data including Wednesday's trade figures pointed to upward revision in that estimate.
The Commerce Department reported earlier that the U.S. trade deficit fell by more than 19 percent in March to $8.5 billion.

"The stabilization of the trade deficit despite surging growth in the United States during the first quarter is concrete evidence of the continuing improvement in the competitiveness of American firms and workers," Ehrlich said.
But that does not mean that there are no problems.

Although the U.S. trade deficit with China tumbled by more than 20 percent in March from February, Ehrlich attributed that to seasonal factors and noted that China is the only major market in the world where U.S. exports are not growing in the long term.

"This export picture remains an object of concern to this administration," he said. The U.S. deficit with Japan grew by more than eight percent in March to $4.6 billion, its highest level since October last year.
"The trade deficit with Japan has moved sideways over the last six months," Ehrlich said.
"The dollar might play some role (in that)," Ehrlich said.
But differences in growth rates between the two countries may be a more important factor, he said.
After "bombastic" growth in the first quarter of last year the Japanese economy slowed, he noted.
"I don't think we're going to see an unraveling of all the games we've made over the last several years because structural reform on the Japanese side is inevitable," Ehrlich said.
The big unanswered question with respect to Japan is whether or not it will be able to sustain economic growth based on domestic demand, Ehrlich said.
"Our concern ... is that Japan will revert to a pattern of allowing the rest of the world to pull it out of a cyclical downturn," he said.
He said it was "not unreasonable" to expect Japanese consumption to fall after the April 1 increase in the value-added tax there.
The U.S. trade deficit with Mexico rose by more than 23 percent in March but Ehrlich instead highlighted the climb in U.S. exports to that country.
"Our ongoing growth in exports to Mexico shows a clear recovery from the 1995 peso crisis," he said. "We look forward to faster growth in Mexico and better trade results."
U.S. exports in March were boosted by shipments of gold and civilian aircraft. Civilian aircraft exports rose by $745 million in March to a record $2.5 billion.
"In the months ahead we should expect to see some fallback in aircraft sales," Ehrlich said.

U.S. imports of cars and car parts tumbled by $1.2 billion in March. Noting that that followed big increases in imports in January and February, Ehrlich attributed the ups and downs to the fallout from strikes last year in Canadian car plants.
